title: An English country house
hook: Duleep lives as a gentleman in Suffolk, far from the Punjab

segments.voice: Yesterday, sarnai, and your line was a boy far away. Which child came to mind? Today, the boy is grown, and further away than ever. Day nine hundred forty-two.

Shotguns crack across a cold, sandy heath in Suffolk. Beaters walk the fields, birds go up, and the gentlemen fire. The host of the shooting party is known as a remarkable shot. He owns the house, the woods and the land around it. He dines with the Prince of Wales. He has been received by Queen Victoria. And he was born a Maharaja of the Punjab. Today: an English country house.
screen: `SHOTGUNS OVER A SUFFOLK HEATH.` → `THE HOST IS A FINE SHOT.` → `BORN A MAHARAJA.`

segments.voice: First, the move to England. In his teens, Duleep Singh was brought to Britain. The Queen took an interest in him, and he was welcomed at court as an exotic and charming guest. He was paid an allowance by the government that had taken his kingdom, and it was never as much as he thought was owed. Second, the house. He bought an estate called Elveden, in Suffolk, and rebuilt the hall. Inside, some of the rooms were made to look like an Indian palace, with carved arches and rich ornament, set in the middle of the English countryside. Outside, he turned the land into a great shooting estate. Third, the life. He married, and his wife, Bamba Müller, had grown up in Cairo. Their children were raised as English gentry. He shot, entertained, spent heavily and fell into debt. From the outside, the picture was complete: an English gentleman with an Indian title. Fourth, what was underneath. The rooms that looked like a palace tell their own story. A man who had everything a country house can offer still built a piece of the home he had lost into its walls. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, which tradition says was written in longing for the Guru's presence, he says his mind yearns for the sight of the Guru, crying out like the rainbird crying for rain, and that he can't sleep or rest without it. Some Sikh readers of Duleep's story hear that ache in the Indian rooms at Elveden. That's today's line.

segments.voice: Two minutes with where you belong. Sit, and let your breath settle. Ask yourself, without hurrying: where do I belong? It might be a place, a kitchen, a street, a country. It might be a person, or a song, or a smell. Let whatever comes, come. Notice if there's a gap between where you live and where you belong, and don't rush to close it. Just breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Elveden, in Suffolk, the estate where Duleep Singh lived as a gentleman, with rooms built to look like an Indian palace he had lost. Today's word.
Your line: far from punjab. Today, think of where you belong, and do one small thing that touches it: a call, a recipe, a song. Day nine hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Elveden Hall in Suffolk is remembered in Sikh history as Duleep Singh's English home, and Sikh visitors to Britain sometimes travel there to see the place where Maharaja Duleep Singh lived.
